proposed.statement: Can the handle \(\mathfrak H^{\mathrm{low}}\) exhibit constants \(\eta\in(0,1-2\alpha)\), \(\varepsilon_R\in(0,\min\{R_f,R_q\})\), and \(c_{\mathrm{sep}}>0\), and construct \(P_{0,n},P_{1,n}\in\mathcal M\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), with fixed \(p_x\), fixed positive \(f_x\), and fixed nonidentical asymmetric laws of \(U_1,U_2\) shared across \(j\in\{0,1\}\) and across \(n\), such that only the Bernoulli conditional means \(b_{j,n,x}\) differ; \(1/4\le b_{j,n,x}(a)\le3/4\) for every \(a\in\mathcal A\); \(\sup_x\|f_x\|_{H^{\beta}}\le R_f-\varepsilon_R\) and \(\max_{j\in\{0,1\}}\sup_x\|f_xb_{j,n,x}\|_{H^{\beta}}\le R_q-\varepsilon_R\); \(\operatorname{TV}(((P_{0,n})_{\mathrm{obs}})^{\otimes n},((P_{1,n})_{\mathrm{obs}})^{\otimes n})\le\eta\); and \(\|\mu_{1,n}-\mu_{0,n}\|_{L^{\infty}(I)}\ge c_{\mathrm{sep}}K_n^{1/2-\beta}\)?

open_obligations.what_is_open: For compatible strict-interior quantitative constants, construct one fixed positive density and fixed nonidentical asymmetric error pair together with Bernoulli marked perturbations satisfying the range and strict Sobolev-slack constraints, achieving \(K_n^{1/2-\beta}\) separation, and having product-experiment total variation below \(\eta<1-2\alpha\).
open_obligations.obstruction: The enlarged index ranges still do not guarantee a nonempty strict-interior fixed-density submodel: necessarily \(\kappa|I|\le1\) and \(R_f\ge(2B_A)^{-1/2}\). For compatible constants, the remaining mathematical barrier is to build a single moment-annihilating packet that simultaneously preserves the Bernoulli range and Sobolev slack and then convert its factorial marked-channel attenuation into a weighted chi-square or Hellinger bound; the frozen core supplies no lower envelope for that conversion. The former \(c_0=1\) obstruction is obsolete because the moment condition now yields the protected neighborhood directly.
open_obligations.attempted: The moment inequality was used to derive a uniform protected neighborhood with \(\nu_*=(2M_e^{1/q_e})^{-1}\) and \(c_*=1/2\). The moment-annihilation route was then carried through the exact marked-channel factorization, giving factorial attenuation on a fixed frequency square. Direct compatibility checks isolate the remaining fixed-density obstruction, but the packet construction and product-Hellinger conversion do not close.
open_obligations.partial_result:
The moment condition itself supplies the protected neighborhood that was formerly assumed.  Let \(Q\) be either error law and let \(\phi_Q(t)=\int e^{itu}\,dQ(u)\).  Since \(q_e>1\), Lyapunov's inequality and the error-moment bound give
\[
 \int |u|\,dQ(u)
 \le \left(\int |u|^{q_e}\,dQ(u)\right)^{1/q_e}
 \le M_e^{1/q_e}.
\]
The inequalities \(|1-e^{iv}|\le |v|\) and \(|z|\ge 1-|1-z|\) therefore imply, for every real \(t\),
\[
 |\phi_Q(t)|
 \ge 1-|1-\phi_Q(t)|
 \ge 1-\int |1-e^{itu}|\,dQ(u)
 \ge 1-|t|M_e^{1/q_e}.
\]
Consequently, with
\[
 \nu_*=(2M_e^{1/q_e})^{-1},
 \qquad c_*=\frac12,
\]
one has \(\inf_{|t|\le\nu_*}|\phi_Q(t)|\ge c_*\), uniformly over the enlarged moment class.  Thus no separate spectral-modulus restriction, and in particular no endpoint obstruction involving an independently specified \(c_0\), remains.

Two necessary compatibility conditions for the requested fixed density remain.  The support and denominator conditions imply
\[
 1=\int_{\mathcal A}f_x(a)\,da
 \ge \int_I f_x(a)\,da
 \ge \kappa |I|.
\]
Moreover, since \(|\mathcal A|=2B_A\), Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 1=\int_{\mathcal A}f_x(a)\,da
 \le (2B_A)^{1/2}\|f_x\|_2,
\]
and hence
\[
 R_f\ge \|f_x\|_{H^\beta}\ge \|f_x\|_2
 \ge (2B_A)^{-1/2}.
\]
The displayed ranges of the quantitative constants do not themselves impose either \(\kappa|I|\le1\) or \(R_f\ge(2B_A)^{-1/2}\); when either fails, the requested fixed-density subexperiment cannot exist.

Conditional on compatible strict-interior fixed nuisances, moment annihilation gives the needed analytic attenuation.  Put \(h_n=f(b_{1,n}-b_{0,n})\), and suppose that
\[
 \int_{\mathcal A}a^k h_n(a)\,da=0,
 \qquad 0\le k<K_n.
\]
For \(|u|\le\Omega\), Taylor's formula for \(e^{iua}\), the support bound \(|a|\le B_A\), and the preceding cancellations yield
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |\widehat h_n(u)|
 &=\left|\int_{\mathcal A}
     \left(e^{iua}-\sum_{k=0}^{K_n-1}\frac{(iua)^k}{k!}\right)
     h_n(a)\,da\right|\\
 &\le \|h_n\|_1 e^{B_A\Omega}
       \frac{(B_A\Omega)^{K_n}}{K_n!}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
By the marked-channel factorization, the two-dimensional Fourier transform of the observed marked-density perturbation equals
\[
 \widehat h_n(s+t)\phi_1(s)\phi_2(t).
\]
For fixed error transforms supported in bounded frequency intervals, this transform is confined to a fixed square and inherits the factorial bound above.  What remains unproved is the simultaneous construction of a packet satisfying the Bernoulli range, strict Sobolev slack, and \(K_n^{1/2-\beta}\) supremum separation, together with a weighted chi-square or Hellinger inequality converting the Fourier attenuation into \(\operatorname{TV}(((P_{0,n})_{\mathrm{obs}})^{\otimes n},((P_{1,n})_{\mathrm{obs}})^{\otimes n})\le\eta\).

prose_updates.tldr: This is a statistical-inference paper about a causal ADRF under two blind nonidentical asymmetric replicates. The fixed quantitative class now allows every \(\beta>1/2\) and every fixed \(q_e>1\); the common moment bound itself supplies a uniform protected frequency neighborhood, so no separate local spectral-modulus restriction is assumed. Analytic cocycle identification and an explicit structural response-surface condition establish the causal identifying functional. Two simultaneous bands are distinguished: an explicit finite relaxed outer-sieve construction is uniformly honest and clipped to \(0\le W_n\le2B_Y\), while an abstract noncomputational exact-class construction is uniformly honest with uniformly \(o(1)\) expected maximal width. Neither construction proves the candidate \(r_n\) rate. The fixed-nuisance Bernoulli lower modulus remains unresolved, so there is no matched honest-band rate.

project_justification.gap: Existing statistical results cover blind repeated-measurement density estimation, confidence bands under auxiliary-error, symmetric-error, or fixed-operator designs, and pointwise continuous-treatment inference. They do not provide a quantitative shrinking rate for a uniformly honest simultaneous ADRF band with blind nonidentical asymmetric replicate errors and possible spectral gaps. The present empirical-grid outer set lacks a quantitative marked inverse modulus, and the fixed-nuisance Bernoulli modulus needed for a sharp all-band converse remains unproved.
project_justification.niche: The inferential niche is a nonlinear severe inverse problem over the full Sobolev-continuity range \(\beta>1/2\). Compact treatment support supplies entire transforms, one centered replicate fixes translation, and the uniform \(q_e>1\) moment bound yields \( |\phi_Q(t)|\ge1-|t|M_e^{1/q_e}\), hence a common near-origin conditioning region without a separate spectral assumption. The causal target is a stratum-weighted quotient. A jointly measurable response surface driven by an exogenous random element and continuity of the stratum-specific causal mean bridge that observed regression quotient to the point-dose causal curve. The distinction between qualitative identification and quantitative confidence-set diameter is essential here.
project_justification.fill: The paper delivers two inference maps over this enlarged class. The explicit map uses deterministic spline, frequency, truncation, and atomic dimensions; simultaneous probability-, marked-, and mass-channel radii; relaxed compact outer signal sieves; moment-constrained error sieves with the derived protected neighborhood; a joint feasible set; and measurable clipped ADRF extrema. It proves uniform simultaneous coverage and \(0\le W_n\le2B_Y\), but no shrinkage. In parallel, exact empirical-channel residuals are profiled over a compact projected nuisance class with no separately imposed local-modulus constraint. Compactness, expanding-grid equality, and marked cocycle injectivity prove that this abstract exact-class band is uniformly honest and has uniformly \(o(1)\) expected maximal width. The qualitative argument supplies no explicit modulus, and the sharp \(O(r_n)\) upper and matching marked converse remain open.

sampling_model.treatment: \(S_{i1}=A_i+U_{i1}\) and \(S_{i2}=A_i+U_{i2}\), with independent errors that need not be identically distributed or symmetric and may have spectral gaps. The class fixes \(q_e>1\) and \(E|U_j|^{q_e}\le M_e\), and only \(E[U_2]=0\) fixes location. The moment bound implies \( |\phi_j(t)|\ge1-|t|M_e^{1/q_e}\), so \(\nu_*=(2M_e^{1/q_e})^{-1}\) and \(c_*=1/2\) give a common protected neighborhood rather than an additional model restriction.
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: The explicit conservative procedure uses relaxed order-\(d\) B-spline families for \(f_x,q_x\), finite atomic error laws satisfying the \(q_e\)-moment and centering restrictions and the moment-derived protected-neighborhood bounds, and \(p_x\in\mathcal P_{n,\alpha}\) against simultaneous empirical probability- and marked-channel restrictions on \(\mathcal D_n\); its outer splines are feasibility devices rather than asserted model laws. A second, abstract procedure profiles the same empirical radii with no approximation allowances over the exact compact projected class \(\mathscr K\), then takes clipped extrema of \(\mu_{\vartheta}\). The latter is an infinite-dimensional existence construction and is not claimed to be computationally implementable.

prose_updates.related_work: Capitao-Miniconi, Gassiat, and Lehéricy provide the unmarked probability-channel cocycle, constrained polynomial estimator, and compact-support \(L^2\) minimax experiment that inform the analytic machinery. Their qualitative H1--H2 identification class has no common error-moment radius and identifies only up to translation; their estimation classes add separate quantitative restrictions, and their Theorem 4 is a latent-density \(L^2\) converse rather than an ADRF-band converse. In the present class, the sole uniform error restriction beyond independence and centering is a fixed \(q_e>1\) moment radius, from which the protected neighborhood is derived. Their rate argument uses a protected-region integrated contrast with nearly parametric forward error and does not supply a Lipschitz inverse for the present grid set whose tolerance contains polynomial Jackson error. Gassiat, Le Corff, and Lehéricy supply the broader analytic-continuation principle for blind deconvolution. Huang and Zhang formulate the error-contaminated continuous-treatment ADRF and derive pointwise inference with a known everywhere-nonzero error transform. Kato and Sasaki (2018) develop deconvolution bands with an unknown error distribution using an auxiliary error sample, together with a symmetric-error repeated-measurement route; that design differs from two blind nonidentical asymmetric replicates and has neither the marked quotient nor joint cell-mass profiling. Kato and Sasaki (2019) obtain multiplier-bootstrap uniform bands under conventional spectral conditions. Kato, Sasaki, and Ura invert Kotlarski restrictions to retain coverage without completeness, but do not establish a shrinking marked-quotient band here. Babii studies honest expected diameter for fixed linear inverse operators. Low supplies a testing-to-expected-length reduction only after a marked modulus is established. None of these sources proves the missing quantitative diameter or fixed-nuisance Bernoulli modulus for the present problem.
prose_updates.interpretation: The observed two-channel law identifies the continuous regression curve \(q_x/f_x\). The common near-zero nonvanishing region used by the cocycle is a consequence of the uniform \(q_e>1\) moment bound, not a separate spectral restriction; open zero sets away from that region remain allowed. Structural exogeneity first equates the regression curve with the stratum-specific causal mean almost everywhere in dose; positivity and continuity then extend the equality to every target dose. Coordinatewise weak unconfoundedness and almost-sure consistency alone would not suffice because they permit treatment-dependent diagonal modifications on null sets.
prose_updates.technical_internal_limitation: The causal bridge, moment-derived protected neighborhood, analytic-cocycle identification, simultaneous transform concentration, uniform Jackson approximation for every \(\beta>1/2\), relaxed outer-sieve embedding, and clipped uniform coverage are established. The finite grid-sieve set has no quantitative inverse modulus and therefore no shrinking-width guarantee. Exact-class compactness over the \(q_e>1\) moment class yields a separate uniformly honest band with uniformly \(o(1)\) expected width, but gives no rate, tuning law, or finite algorithm. The sharp-rate program still requires a protected-cube analytic-polynomial confidence construction for both probability and signed marked channels. On the lower side, compatible strict-interior fixed nuisances, a Bernoulli-range Sobolev packet, and a weighted Hellinger or chi-square conversion remain unresolved; the former independently specified \(c_0=1\) obstruction has disappeared with deletion of the separate local-modulus assumption.
prose_updates.honest_scope: The enlarged fixed quantitative model has compact dose support, bounded outcomes, Sobolev radii with \(\beta>1/2\), overlap, finite-stratum positivity, a fixed \(q_e>1\) error-moment radius, centering of the second error, and the structural causal response surface. It imposes no separate local spectral-modulus restriction: \(\nu_*=(2M_e^{1/q_e})^{-1}\) and \(c_*=1/2\) follow uniformly from the moment bound. The explicit finite relaxed outer-sieve band is uniformly honest for all sufficiently large \(n\) and universally clipped to width at most \(2B_Y\), with no proved shrinkage. The parallel exact-class band is abstract and noncomputational; it is uniformly honest and its expected maximal width is uniformly \(o(1)\), but no explicit rate follows. In particular, no \(O(r_n)\), minimax-matching, or rate-elbow claim is made. The matching-converse kernel remains open as \(\mathrm{oeq{:}fixed\text{-}nuisance\text{-}marked\text{-}modulus}\).

proofs.proof_tex:
Put \(m=|\mathcal X|\) and
\[
 e_{p,n}=\left\{\frac{\log(6m/\alpha)}{2n}\right\}^{1/2}.
\]
We first prove the concentration statement.  If \(Z\in[0,1]\) and \(\psi(\lambda)=\log E\exp\{\lambda(Z-EZ)\}\), exponential tilting gives \(\psi''(\lambda)=\operatorname{Var}_{\lambda}(Z)\).  Every tilted law remains supported on \([0,1]\), so
\[
 \operatorname{Var}_{\lambda}(Z)
 \le E_{\lambda}\{(Z-1/2)^2\}\le\frac14.
\]
Together with \(\psi(0)=\psi'(0)=0\), two integrations yield
\[
 \log E\exp\{\lambda(Z-EZ)\}\le\frac{\lambda^2}{8},
 \qquad \lambda\in\mathbb R.                                    \tag{1}
\]
For each \(x\in\mathcal X\), assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}iid}\) makes \(\widehat p_x\) the average of \(n\) independent Bernoulli variables with common mean \(p_x\).  Exponential Markov inequality, (1), and optimization give
\[
 P_{\mathrm{obs}}^{\otimes n}
 \bigl(|\widehat p_x-p_x|>e_{p,n}\bigr)
 \le2e^{-2ne_{p,n}^2}=\frac{\alpha}{3m}.                          \tag{2}
\]
The union bound over the finite set \(\mathcal X\) therefore gives
\[
 P_{\mathrm{obs}}^{\otimes n}
 \left(\max_{x\in\mathcal X}|\widehat p_x-p_x|\le e_{p,n}\right)
 \ge1-\frac\alpha3.                                               \tag{3}
\]
The true mass vector is nonnegative and sums to one.  Hence, by \(\mathrm{def{:}mass\text{-}confidence\text{-}region}\), the event in (3) is exactly \(\{(p_x)_{x\in\mathcal X}\in\mathcal P_{n,\alpha}\}\), and the asserted coordinate bound is part of the same definition.

For the cell-count assertion, let \(N\) be binomial with parameters \(n\) and \(p\).  For \(t>0\), exponential Markov inequality and \(1-p+pe^{-t}\le\exp\{p(e^{-t}-1)\}\) imply
\[
 \Pr(N\le np/2)
 \le\exp\{tnp/2+np(e^{-t}-1)\}.
\]
Taking \(t=\log2\) makes the exponent \(-np(1-\log2)/2\le-np/8\).  Since \(n_x\) is binomial with parameters \(n\) and \(p_x\), assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}strata}\) and a union bound give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 P_{\mathrm{obs}}^{\otimes n}
 \left(\min_{x\in\mathcal X}n_x<np_{\min}/2\right)
 &\le\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}
 P_{\mathrm{obs}}^{\otimes n}(n_x<np_x/2)\\
 &\le m e^{-np_{\min}/8}.                                       \tag{4}
 \end{aligned}
\]

It remains to bound mass profiling.  Let \(p=(p_x)\) and \(p'=(p'_x)\) belong to \(\mathcal P_{n,\alpha}\), and fix \(f_x\in\mathscr F_n\) and \(q_x\in\mathscr Q_n(f_x)\) in every cell.  Put \(e_n=a_{q,n}+B_Ya_{f,n}\).  The continuum constraints in \(\mathrm{def{:}signal\text{-}sieves}\) give, for \(a\in I\),
\[
 f_x(a)\ge\kappa/2,
 \qquad |q_x(a)|\le B_Yf_x(a)+e_n.
\]
The denominator is therefore strictly positive, and \(b_{\mu,n}=4e_n/\kappa\) gives
\[
 \left|\frac{q_x(a)}{f_x(a)}\right|
 \le B_Y+\frac{2e_n}{\kappa}
 =B_Y+\frac{b_{\mu,n}}2.                                         \tag{5}
\]
Both mass vectors are within \(e_{p,n}\) of \(\widehat p\) coordinatewise.  Thus (5) and the triangle inequality imply
\[
 \sup_{a\in I}\left|
 \sum_{x\in\mathcal X}(p_x-p'_x)\frac{q_x(a)}{f_x(a)}
 \right|
 \le2m\left(B_Y+\frac{b_{\mu,n}}2\right)e_{p,n}.                \tag{6}
\]
Finally put \(\gamma=\beta-1/2>0\).  The tuning definitions in \(\mathrm{def{:}upper\text{-}tuning\text{-}grid}\) and \(\mathrm{def{:}ecf\text{-}radii}\) give
\[
 K_n\sim\frac{\log n}{\log\log n},\qquad
 b_{\mu,n}=O(K_n^{-\gamma})=O(r_n).
\]
Since \(m,\alpha,B_Y\), and all class radii are fixed,
\[
 \log\left(\frac{e_{p,n}}{r_n}\right)
 =-\frac12\log n+\gamma\log\!\left(\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}\right)+O(1)
 \longrightarrow-\infty.                                        \tag{7}
\]
Also \(b_{\mu,n}=o(1)\).  Equations (6)--(7) therefore show that its right-hand side is \(o(r_n)\).  This uses exactly \(\gamma>0\), equivalently \(\beta>1/2\), and proves the claim throughout the enlarged smoothness range.

Fix \(P\in\mathcal M\) and \(x\in\mathcal X\).  Apply \(\mathrm{lem{:}sobolev\text{-}spline\text{-}jackson}\) to \(f_x\) and \(q_x\).  Their common support is contained in \(\mathcal A\) by \(\mathrm{ass{:}compact\text{-}dose}\), the identity \(q_x=m_xf_x\), and the fact that \(f_x=0\) almost everywhere off \(\mathcal A\).  Assumptions \(\mathrm{ass{:}f\text{-}sobolev}\) and \(\mathrm{ass{:}q\text{-}sobolev}\), together with \(\mathrm{def{:}ecf\text{-}radii}\), consequently yield splines \(\widetilde f_{x,n}\) and \(\widetilde q_{x,n}\) in the stated order-\(d\) spline space satisfying
\[
 \|\widetilde f_{x,n}-f_x\|_{L^\infty(\mathcal A)}\le a_{f,n},
 \qquad
 \|\widetilde q_{x,n}-q_x\|_{L^\infty(\mathcal A)}\le a_{q,n}. \tag{1}
\]
Because \(K_n\to\infty\) and \(\beta>1/2\), one has \(a_{f,n}\to0\); in particular, \(a_{f,n}<\kappa/2\) for all sufficiently large \(n\).

The function \(f_x\) is nonnegative and integrates to one over \(\mathcal A\), by its definition as the conditional density and \(\mathrm{ass{:}compact\text{-}dose}\).  Thus (1) and \(\mathrm{ass{:}denominator}\) give
\[
 \widetilde f_{x,n}(a)\ge-a_{f,n}\quad(a\in\mathcal A),
 \qquad
 \widetilde f_{x,n}(a)\ge\kappa-a_{f,n}\ge\kappa/2\quad(a\in I), \tag{2}
\]
and
\[
 \left|\int_{\mathcal A}\widetilde f_{x,n}(a)\,da-1\right|
 \le\int_{\mathcal A}|\widetilde f_{x,n}(a)-f_x(a)|\,da
 \le2B_Aa_{f,n}.                                                   \tag{3}
\]

The common-event representation in \(\mathrm{ass{:}structural\text{-}response\text{-}surface}\), whose response map takes values in \([-B_Y,B_Y]\), and \(\mathrm{ass{:}consistency}\) imply \(|Y|\le B_Y\) almost surely.  Conditional Jensen inequality therefore gives \(|m_x(a)|\le B_Y\) for \(f_x(a)\,da\)-almost every \(a\), and hence \(|q_x|\le B_Yf_x\) almost everywhere.  For completeness, \(\beta>1/2\) makes the Sobolev representatives continuous: by Cauchy--Schwarz,
\[
 \int|\widehat g(t)|\,dt
 \le\|g\|_{H^\beta}
 \left\{\int(1+t^2)^{-\beta}\,dt\right\}^{1/2}<\infty,
\]
so Fourier inversion gives a continuous representative.  The almost-everywhere envelope thus extends to every \(a\in\mathcal A\).  Using (1),
\[
 |\widetilde q_{x,n}(a)|
 \le |q_x(a)|+a_{q,n}
 \le B_Y\widetilde f_{x,n}(a)+a_{q,n}+B_Ya_{f,n},
 \qquad a\in\mathcal A.                                           \tag{4}
\]
Equations (2)--(4) are exactly the relaxed constraints in \(\mathrm{def{:}signal\text{-}sieves}\).  Hence \(\widetilde f_{x,n}\in\mathscr F_n\) and \(\widetilde q_{x,n}\in\mathscr Q_n(\widetilde f_{x,n})\).

The outer families are compact at each fixed \(n\).  Their continuum inequalities are closed in the finite-dimensional spline space.  If \(f\in\mathscr F_n\) and \(f_- =\max\{-f,0\}\), then
\[
 \int_{\mathcal A}|f|
 =\int_{\mathcal A}f+2\int_{\mathcal A}f_-
 \le1+6B_Aa_{f,n},                                                 \tag{5}
\]
because \(f_-\le a_{f,n}\) and \(|\int_{\mathcal A}f-1|\le2B_Aa_{f,n}\).  The marked envelope then bounds \(\int_{\mathcal A}|q|\) uniformly.  Norm equivalence in the fixed finite-dimensional spline spaces bounds all coefficients.  The two closed families are therefore bounded and compact.  No exact-density or shape-preserving projection is used.

It remains to compare the profiled quotient with the causal target.  The established \(\mathrm{thm{:}adrf\text{-}id}\) gives \(\mu(a)=\sum_xp_xq_x(a)/f_x(a)\) on \(I\).  For \(a\in I\), (1)--(2), \(f_x(a)\ge\kappa\), and \(|q_x(a)|\le B_Yf_x(a)\) imply
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \left|\frac{\widetilde q_{x,n}(a)}{\widetilde f_{x,n}(a)}
       -\frac{q_x(a)}{f_x(a)}\right|
 &\le\frac{|\widetilde q_{x,n}(a)-q_x(a)|}{\widetilde f_{x,n}(a)}
 +\frac{|q_x(a)|\,|\widetilde f_{x,n}(a)-f_x(a)|}
 {f_x(a)\widetilde f_{x,n}(a)}\\
 &\le\frac{a_{q,n}+B_Ya_{f,n}}{\kappa-a_{f,n}}\\
 &\le2\kappa^{-1}(a_{q,n}+B_Ya_{f,n}).                            \tag{6}
 \end{aligned}
\]
The nonnegative masses sum to one, so summing (6) proves
\[
 \sup_{a\in I}\left|
 \sum_{x\in\mathcal X}p_x
 \frac{\widetilde q_{x,n}(a)}{\widetilde f_{x,n}(a)}-\mu(a)
 \right|
 \le2\kappa^{-1}(a_{q,n}+B_Ya_{f,n})
 \le b_{\mu,n},
\]
where the last inequality is the definition in \(\mathrm{def{:}ecf\text{-}radii}\).

Fix \(P\in\mathcal M\), \(j\in\{1,2\}\), and \(n\).  Define
\[
 U_j^H=\max\{-H_n,\min\{U_j,H_n\}\}.
\]
Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}error\text{-}moment}\) and \(\mathbf 1\{|U_j|>H_n\}\le |U_j|^{q_e}H_n^{-q_e}\) give
\[
 P(|U_j|>H_n)\le M_eH_n^{-q_e}.
\]
Consequently, for every real \(t\),
\[
 \left|E_Pe^{itU_j^H}-\phi_j(t)\right|
 \le2P(|U_j|>H_n)
 \le2M_eH_n^{-q_e}=\tau_{e,n},                                    \tag{1}
\]
and clipping gives
\[
 E_P|U_j^H|^{q_e}\le E_P|U_j|^{q_e}\le M_e.                       \tag{2}
\]
For \(j=2\), \(\mathrm{ass{:}center\text{-}two}\), \(q_e>1\), and \(|u|\mathbf 1\{|u|>H_n\}\le |u|^{q_e}H_n^{1-q_e}\) give
\[
 |E_PU_2^H|
 =|E_P(U_2^H-U_2)|
 \le M_eH_n^{1-q_e}.                                               \tag{3}
\]

Put \(D=2|\Gamma_n|+2\), and define the continuous map
\[
 v(u)=\bigl((\operatorname{Re}e^{itu},\operatorname{Im}e^{itu})_{t\in\Gamma_n},u,|u|^{q_e}\bigr)
 \in\mathbb R^D.
\]
The vector \(E_Pv(U_j^H)\) lies in the convex hull of the compact set \(v([-H_n,H_n])\): finite simple-function approximations to the integral lie in that convex hull, and a convex hull of a compact subset of a finite-dimensional space is compact.

We give the finite-support reduction explicitly.  If a convex representation uses more than \(D+1\) points, the augmented vectors \((1,v(u_r))\in\mathbb R^{D+1}\) are linearly dependent.  Thus coefficients \(a_r\), not all zero, satisfy \(\sum_ra_r=0\) and \(\sum_ra_rv(u_r)=0\).  After changing the common sign if necessary, some \(a_r>0\).  Subtracting \(c(a_r)_r\) from the weights, where \(c=\min_{a_r>0}w_r/a_r\), preserves their sum and barycenter, keeps all weights nonnegative, and makes at least one weight zero.  Iteration leaves at most
\[
 D+1=2|\Gamma_n|+3\le M_n
\]
atoms.  Padding with zero-weight atoms at \(H_n\) and ordering the locations produces an atomic characteristic function \(\bar\phi_{j,n}\) that agrees with \(E_Pe^{itU_j^H}\) at every \(t\in\Gamma_n\), has the same mean and \(q_e\)-moment, and is supported on \([-H_n,H_n]\).  Equations (1)--(3) yield
\[
 \max_{t\in\Gamma_n}|\bar\phi_{j,n}(t)-\phi_j(t)|\le\tau_{e,n}, \tag{4}
\]
and, for \(j=2\),
\[
 \left|\sum_{\ell=1}^{M_n}w_{2\ell}u_{2\ell}\right|
 \le M_eH_n^{1-q_e}.                                               \tag{5}
\]

It remains only to check the explicit protected-neighborhood constraint in the corrected \(\mathrm{def{:}error\text{-}sieves}\).  By (2), the atomic law satisfies \(\sum_\ell w_{j\ell}|u_{j\ell}|^{q_e}\le M_e\).  Applying \(\mathrm{lem{:}moment\text{-}derived\text{-}protected\text{-}neighborhood}\) to this atomic law gives directly
\[
 \inf_{|t|\le\nu_*}|\bar\phi_{j,n}(t)|\ge c_*.                    \tag{6}
\]
Thus the support, probability-weight, moment, and protected-frequency restrictions of \(\widetilde\Phi_{j,n}\) all hold.  For \(j=2\), (5) is stronger than the additional bound \(2M_eH_n^{1-q_e}\) defining \(\Phi_{2,n}\).  Hence \(\bar\phi_{j,n}\in\Phi_{j,n}\), and (4)--(5) prove the result.  The threshold \(q_e>1\) is used exactly in (3), where it makes the centering error vanish as \(H_n\to\infty\); no separately assumed spectral modulus is used.

Fix a sufficiently large \(n\).  Conditional on \((X_i)_{i=1}^n\), the observations in every nonempty cell are independent with the conditional law given \(X=x\), by \(\mathrm{ass{:}iid}\).  Each real and imaginary part of a probability-channel summand lies in \([-1,1]\).  The common-event bounded response in \(\mathrm{ass{:}structural\text{-}response\text{-}surface}\) and \(\mathrm{ass{:}consistency}\) give \(|Y|\le B_Y\) almost surely, so each real and imaginary part of a marked-channel summand lies in \([-B_Y,B_Y]\).

Apply the moment-generating-function calculation in \(\mathrm{lem{:}mass\text{-}confidence}\), rescaled to an interval of length \(2c\), separately to real and imaginary parts.  Since \(|z|>u\) implies \(\max\{|\operatorname{Re}z|,|\operatorname{Im}z|\}>u/\sqrt2\), when \(n_x>\lambda_n\), for every \((s,t)\in\mathcal D_n\),
\[
 \Pr\left(
 |\widehat F_{x,n}(s,t)-F_x(s,t)|>2\sqrt{\lambda_n/n_x}
 \ \middle|\ (X_i)_{i=1}^n\right)\le4e^{-\lambda_n},             \tag{1}
\]
and
\[
 \Pr\left(
 |\widehat G_{x,n}(s,t)-G_x(s,t)|>2B_Y\sqrt{\lambda_n/n_x}
 \ \middle|\ (X_i)_{i=1}^n\right)\le4e^{-\lambda_n}.            \tag{2}
\]
If \(n_x\le\lambda_n\), the empirical-channel definitions, including the empty-cell convention, and \(|F_x|\le1\), \(|G_x|\le B_Y\) show deterministically that the deviations are bounded by \(\rho^F_{x,n}=2\) and \(\rho^G_{x,n}=2B_Y\).  A conditional union bound over both channels, every cell, and every grid point has failure probability at most
\[
 8|\mathcal X||\mathcal D_n|e^{-\lambda_n}=\alpha/6.              \tag{3}
\]
Combining (3) with the mass-region failure probability \(\alpha/3\) from \(\mathrm{lem{:}mass\text{-}confidence}\), and integrating over the labels, gives uniformly over \(P\in\mathcal M\),
\[
 P_{\mathrm{obs}}^{\otimes n}(\mathcal E_{n,\alpha})
 \ge1-\alpha/3-\alpha/6\ge1-\alpha.                              \tag{4}
\]

Suppose that \(\mathcal E_{n,\alpha}\) occurs.  Apply \(\mathrm{lem{:}outer\text{-}spline\text{-}embedding}\) in every cell and \(\mathrm{lem{:}atomic\text{-}grid\text{-}embedding}\) to both error laws, the latter now using the moment-derived protected neighborhood.  Define
\[
 \bar\theta_n=
 \bigl((p_x,\widetilde f_{x,n},\widetilde q_{x,n})_{x\in\mathcal X},
       \bar\phi_{1,n},\bar\phi_{2,n}\bigr).
\]
Its mass vector belongs to \(\mathcal P_{n,\alpha}\).  If \((s,t)\in\mathcal D_n\), then \(s,t\in\Gamma_n\).  Characteristic functions have modulus at most one.  Also \(|\widehat f_x(u)|\le1\), and \(|\widehat q_x(u)|\le\int|q_x|\le B_Y\), because \(|q_x|\le B_Yf_x\) and \(f_x\) is a density.  Uniform approximation on \(\mathcal A\) gives
\[
 |\widehat{\widetilde f}_{x,n}(u)-\widehat f_x(u)|\le2B_Aa_{f,n},
 \qquad
 |\widehat{\widetilde q}_{x,n}(u)-\widehat q_x(u)|\le2B_Aa_{q,n}. \tag{5}
\]
At grid points, the atomic embedding gives
\[
 |\bar\phi_{1,n}(s)\bar\phi_{2,n}(t)-\phi_1(s)\phi_2(t)|
 \le|\bar\phi_{1,n}(s)-\phi_1(s)|
   +|\bar\phi_{2,n}(t)-\phi_2(t)|
 \le2\tau_{e,n}.                                                   \tag{6}
\]
The established factorization lemma, (5)--(6), and the triangle inequality now give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \left|\widehat{\widetilde f}_{x,n}(s+t)
 \bar\phi_{1,n}(s)\bar\phi_{2,n}(t)-F_x(s,t)\right|
 &\le2B_Aa_{f,n}+2\tau_{e,n}\le\delta^F_n,\\
 \left|\widehat{\widetilde q}_{x,n}(s+t)
 \bar\phi_{1,n}(s)\bar\phi_{2,n}(t)-G_x(s,t)\right|
 &\le2B_Aa_{q,n}+2B_Y\tau_{e,n}\le\delta^G_n.                   \tag{7}
 \end{aligned}
\]
Combining (7) with the empirical inequalities defining \(\mathcal E_{n,\alpha}\) verifies every residual constraint in \(\mathrm{def{:}joint\text{-}feasible\text{-}set}\); the embedding lemmas verify every deterministic sieve constraint.  Hence
\[
 \bar\theta_n\in\Theta_{n,\alpha}.                               \tag{8}
\]
The quotient conclusion of \(\mathrm{lem{:}outer\text{-}spline\text{-}embedding}\), with the true mass vector, gives
\[
 \|\mu_{\bar\theta_n}-\mu\|_{L^\infty(I)}\le b_{\mu,n}.       \tag{9}
\]

Finally consider an arbitrary realized sample.  Put \(e_n=a_{q,n}+B_Ya_{f,n}\).  For any \(\theta\in\Theta_{n,\alpha}\), the simplex constraint, the marked outer envelope, and \(f_x\ge\kappa/2\) on \(I\) yield
\[
 |\mu_\theta(a)|
 \le\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}p_x
 \left(B_Y+\frac{e_n}{f_x(a)}\right)
 \le B_Y+\frac{2e_n}{\kappa}
 =B_Y+\frac{b_{\mu,n}}2.                                         \tag{10}
\]
If the feasible set is nonempty, put \(\ell(a)=\inf_{\theta\in\Theta_{n,\alpha}}\mu_\theta(a)\) and \(u(a)=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_{n,\alpha}}\mu_\theta(a)\).  Equation (10) and \(\ell(a)\le u(a)\) imply
\[
 \ell(a)-b_{\mu,n}\le B_Y,
 \qquad -B_Y\le u(a)+b_{\mu,n},
 \qquad \ell(a)-b_{\mu,n}\le u(a)+b_{\mu,n}.                   \tag{11}
\]
Together with \(-B_Y\le B_Y\), these inequalities show
\[
 \max\{-B_Y,\ell(a)-b_{\mu,n}\}
 \le\min\{B_Y,u(a)+b_{\mu,n}\}.
\]
Both endpoints lie in \([-B_Y,B_Y]\).  If the feasible set is empty, both endpoints equal zero by \(\mathrm{def{:}profiled\text{-}band}\).  Therefore, for every sample,
\[
 L_n(a)\le U_n(a)\quad(a\in I),
 \qquad 0\le W_n\le2B_Y.                                         \tag{12}
\]
Equations (4), (8), (9), and (12) prove exactly the simultaneous confidence, outer embedding, ADRF approximation, and clipping conclusions.  The argument uses \(\beta>1/2\), \(q_e>1\), and the moment-derived protected neighborhood; it uses no separately assumed local spectral modulus and proves no inverse-diameter rate.

added_lemmas.statement:
For every \(\beta>1/2\), with \(d=\lceil\beta\rceil+1\), there is a finite constant \(C_{\beta,\mathcal A}\), depending only on \(\beta\), \(\mathcal A\), and the fixed normalized order-\(d\) B-spline convention, such that the following holds.  If \(g\in H^\beta(\mathbb R)\) is supported on \(\mathcal A\), then, for every sufficiently large \(n\), there is a spline \(s_n\) in the span of \(\{\mathsf B_{k,K_n}:1\le k\le K_n+d\}\), extended by zero off \(\mathcal A\), for which
\[
 \|g-s_n\|_{L^\infty(\mathcal A)}
 \le C_{\beta,\mathcal A}K_n^{1/2-\beta}
       \|g\|_{H^\beta(\mathbb R)}.
\]
The same constant works for all \(g\) in the stated Sobolev space; only finitely many one-sided boundary-stencil patterns occur.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Fix a sufficiently large \(n\), put \(K=K_n\) and \(h=2B_A/K\), and let \(N_d\) be the cardinal B-spline of order \(d\), normalized so that its integer translates form a partition of unity.  We first construct a fixed local quasi-interpolant.  For every polynomial \(p\) of degree less than \(d\), the convolution identity \(N_d=N_{d-1}*\mathbf 1_{[0,1]}\), induction on \(d\), and the binomial formula show that
\[
 y\longmapsto \sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}k^rN_d(y-k),
 \qquad 0\le r<d,
\]
is a polynomial of degree \(r\) with leading coefficient one.  Thus the moment matrix taking the coefficients of a polynomial of degree less than \(d\) to these \(d\) discrete moments is triangular with unit diagonal.  Inverting this fixed matrix gives coefficient functionals \(\lambda_k\), each a fixed finite linear combination of point evaluations on a stencil of size depending only on \(d\), such that
\[
 Q_hg(x):=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}\lambda_k(g)N_d(x/h-k)
 \quad\text{satisfies}\quad Q_hp=p
 \quad\text{for every }p\in\mathbb P_{d-1}.                 \tag{1}
\]
At any fixed \(x\), only a number of terms depending on \(d\) is nonzero.  The inverse moment matrix is fixed, so there is \(C_d<\infty\) such that
\[
 |Q_hg(x)|\le C_d\max\{|g(v)|:|v-x|\le C_dh\}.              \tag{2}
\]
Apply (1)--(2) to \(e_\xi(v)=e^{i\xi v}\).  When \(|h\xi|\le1\), expand the exponential at \(x\) through degree \(d-1\).  The polynomial part cancels by (1), while the integral Taylor remainder is at most a constant times \(|h\xi|^d\) on every point in the fixed stencil.  When \(|h\xi|>1\), (2) and \(|e_\xi|=1\) give a constant bound.  Hence
\[
 \sup_{x\in\mathbb R}|e^{i\xi x}-Q_he_\xi(x)|
 \le C_d\min\{1,(h|\xi|)^d\}.                              \tag{3}
\]

Because \(\beta>1/2\), Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 \int_{\mathbb R}|\widehat g(\xi)|\,d\xi
 \le \|g\|_{H^\beta}
 \left\{\int_{\mathbb R}(1+\xi^2)^{-\beta}\,d\xi\right\}^{1/2}
 <\infty.                                                     \tag{4}
\]
Fourier inversion, the locality of \(Q_h\), and (4) permit termwise application of \(Q_h\).  Therefore (3) and Cauchy--Schwarz imply
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \|g-Q_hg\|_\infty
 &\le C_d\int_{\mathbb R}
       \min\{1,(h|\xi|)^d\}|\widehat g(\xi)|\,d\xi\\
 &\le C_d\|g\|_{H^\beta}
 \left\{\int_{\mathbb R}\min\{1,(h|\xi|)^{2d}\}
                  (1+\xi^2)^{-\beta}\,d\xi\right\}^{1/2}.
                                                                  \tag{5}
 \end{aligned}
\]
For \(0<h\le1\), split the last integral at \(|\xi|=h^{-1}\).  Since \(d=\lceil\beta\rceil+1>\beta-1/2\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &\int_{|\xi|\le h^{-1}}(h|\xi|)^{2d}(1+\xi^2)^{-\beta}\,d\xi
 \le C_{\beta,d}h^{2\beta-1},\\
 &\int_{|\xi|>h^{-1}}(1+\xi^2)^{-\beta}\,d\xi
 \le C_\beta h^{2\beta-1}.                                    \tag{6}
 \end{aligned}
\]
Indeed, on \(1\le|\xi|\le h^{-1}\) the first integrand is bounded by \(h^{2d}|\xi|^{2d-2\beta}\), whose integral is \(O(h^{2\beta-1})\); on \(|\xi|\le1\) it is \(O(h^{2d})=O(h^{2\beta-1})\), and the second line is the elementary tail integral, finite because \(\beta>1/2\).  Equations (5)--(6) give
\[
 \|g-Q_hg\|_\infty\le C_{\beta,d}h^{\beta-1/2}\|g\|_{H^\beta}.
                                                                  \tag{7}
\]

Extend \(g\) by zero off \(\mathcal A\), as it already is by the support premise, and restrict \(Q_hg\) to \(\mathcal A\).  This restriction is a spline of order \(d\) on the uniform partition.  Only the stencils meeting either endpoint differ from the interior translation pattern; there are at most \(2d\) such stencils and hence only finitely many boundary patterns.  Under the fixed clamped normalized basis convention, the restriction is in the span of \(\{\mathsf B_{k,K_n}:1\le k\le K_n+d\}\); extending that restriction by zero is exactly an admissible sieve spline.  Taking \(s_n=(Q_hg)|_{\mathcal A}\), substituting \(h=2B_A/K_n\) in (7), and absorbing \((2B_A)^{\beta-1/2}\) and the finitely many boundary constants into \(C_{\beta,\mathcal A}\) proves the assertion uniformly over \(g\).

added_lemmas.statement:
Let \(j\in\{1,2\}\), and let \(Q_j\) be any Borel probability law on \(\mathbb R\) satisfying \(\int |u|^{q_e}\,dQ_j(u)\le M_e\), where \(q_e>1\).  Then
\[
 |\phi_{Q_j}(t)|\ge 1-|t|M_e^{1/q_e}\qquad(t\in\mathbb R).
\]
Consequently, for \(\nu_*=(2M_e^{1/q_e})^{-1}\) and \(c_*=1/2\),
\[
 \inf_{|t|\le\nu_*}|\phi_{Q_j}(t)|\ge c_*.
\]
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
The probability normalization gives \(\phi_{Q_j}(0)=1\).  Lyapunov's inequality, whose present one-dimensional form follows from Jensen's inequality applied to the concave map \(z\mapsto z^{1/q_e}\), gives
\[
 \int |u|\,dQ_j(u)
 \le\left\{\int |u|^{q_e}\,dQ_j(u)\right\}^{1/q_e}
 \le M_e^{1/q_e}.                                                \tag{1}
\]
For real \(v\), the fundamental theorem of calculus gives \(|e^{iv}-1|\le|v|\).  Hence the reverse triangle inequality and (1) yield, for every real \(t\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |\phi_{Q_j}(t)|
 &\ge 1-|\phi_{Q_j}(t)-1|\\
 &\ge 1-\int|e^{itu}-1|\,dQ_j(u)\\
 &\ge 1-|t|\int|u|\,dQ_j(u)
 \ge 1-|t|M_e^{1/q_e}.                                          \tag{2}
 \end{aligned}
\]
If \(|t|\le\nu_*=(2M_e^{1/q_e})^{-1}\), the last member of (2) is at least \(1/2=c_*\), proving the claimed uniform protected neighborhood.

proofs.proof_tex:
By \(\textnormal{def:exact-projected-class}\), every signal coordinate is supported in the common compact interval \(\mathcal A=[-B_A,B_A]\), and its \(H^\beta\)-norm is bounded by \(R_f\) or \(R_q\).  We first prove compactness of these signal coordinates using only \(\beta>1/2\).  Adopt the Fourier convention
\[
 \|g\|_{H^\beta}^2
 =\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R}(1+t^2)^\beta
       |\widehat g(t)|^2\,dt.
 \tag{1}
\]
For a smooth \(g\), Fourier inversion and Cauchy--Schwarz give
\[
 |g(a)|
 \le \frac{\|g\|_{H^\beta}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
       \left\{\int_{\mathbb R}(1+t^2)^{-\beta}\,dt\right\}^{1/2}
 \tag{2}
\]
and
\[
 |g(a)-g(b)|
 \le \frac{\|g\|_{H^\beta}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
 \left\{\int_{\mathbb R}|e^{-ita}-e^{-itb}|^2
                 (1+t^2)^{-\beta}\,dt\right\}^{1/2}.
 \tag{3}
\]
Smooth approximation in \(H^\beta\) extends (2)--(3) to every \(g\in H^\beta(\mathbb R)\) and supplies its continuous representative.  The integral in (2) is finite precisely because \(\beta>1/2\).  In (3), the integrand converges pointwise to zero as \(|a-b|\to0\) and is bounded by the integrable function \(4(1+t^2)^{-\beta}\).  Splitting the integral at a fixed frequency radius, using uniform convergence on the bounded part and then making the tail small, shows that the right-hand side of (3) tends to zero uniformly over each fixed-radius Sobolev ball.  Thus such a ball is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous on \(\mathcal A\).

We spell out total boundedness.  Given \(\epsilon>0\), choose a finite mesh of \(\mathcal A\) so fine that the common modulus from (3) is at most \(\epsilon/3\) between neighboring mesh points, and quantize the uniformly bounded function values at those points in increments at most \(\epsilon/3\).  Only finitely many quantized arrays occur.  If two functions have the same array, applying (3) from an arbitrary point to a nearest mesh point shows that their uniform distance is at most \(\epsilon\).  One representative from each nonempty array is therefore a finite \(\epsilon\)-net.

The relevant balls are also closed in the uniform topology.  Suppose that \(g_m\) is supported in \(\mathcal A\), \(\|g_m\|_{H^\beta}\le R\), and \(g_m\to g\) uniformly on \(\mathcal A\).  Every continuous zero extension \(g_m\) vanishes at the boundary of \(\mathcal A\); consequently the zero extension of \(g\) is continuous and
\[
 \|g_m-g\|_{L^2(\mathbb R)}
 \le (2B_A)^{1/2}\|g_m-g\|_{L^\infty(\mathcal A)}
 \longrightarrow0.
 \tag{4}
\]
Set \(h_m(t)=(1+t^2)^{\beta/2}\widehat g_m(t)\).  By (1), \((h_m)\) is bounded in \(L^2(\mathbb R)\).  Diagonal selection of its coefficients in a countable orthonormal basis gives a subsequence \(h_{m_k}\) and coefficients defining \(h\in L^2(\mathbb R)\) such that
\[
 h_{m_k}\rightharpoonup h,
 \qquad
 \|h\|_2\le\liminf_{k\to\infty}\|h_{m_k}\|_2.
 \tag{5}
\]
Indeed, boundedness gives coefficientwise subsequences; Bessel's inequality bounds the limiting coefficients, and approximation of an arbitrary \(L^2\) test function by finite basis sums proves weak convergence.  By (4) and the Fourier isometry, \(\widehat g_{m_k}\to\widehat g\) strongly in \(L^2\).  Multiplication by \((1+t^2)^{-\beta/2}\) is bounded on \(L^2\), whereas
\[
 \widehat g_{m_k}=(1+t^2)^{-\beta/2}h_{m_k}
 \rightharpoonup(1+t^2)^{-\beta/2}h.
\]
Uniqueness of the weak limit yields \(\widehat g=(1+t^2)^{-\beta/2}h\).  Hence \(g\in H^\beta(\mathbb R)\), and (5) gives \(\|g\|_{H^\beta}\le R\).  A uniformly Cauchy sequence of continuous functions on \(\mathcal A\) has a pointwise limit and converges to it uniformly, so the uniform function space is complete.  Closedness and total boundedness therefore prove compactness of each fixed-support Sobolev ball in the uniform metric.

Apply this conclusion with \(R=R_f\) and \(R=R_q\).  Uniform convergence on the common support preserves nonnegativity and the unit-integral constraint because
\[
 \left|\int_{\mathcal A}(f_m-f)\right|
 \le 2B_A\|f_m-f\|_{L^\infty(\mathcal A)}.
 \tag{6}
\]
It also preserves \(f_x\ge\kappa\) on \(I\) and \(|q_x|\le B_Yf_x\) on \(\mathbb R\).  Thus the joint signal-coordinate set in \(\mathscr K\) is a closed subset of a finite product of compact spaces and is compact.  The mass vectors form a closed subset of the finite-dimensional simplex because \(p_x\ge p_{\min}\) and \(\sum_xp_x=1\), so that coordinate set is compact as well.

We next prove compactness of each error-law coordinate using only \(q_e>1\).  Let \((Q_m)\) satisfy the moment restriction in \(\textnormal{def:exact-projected-class}\).  For every \(R>0\), integration of \(\mathbf 1\{|u|>R\}\le |u|^{q_e}R^{-q_e}\) gives
\[
 \sup_m Q_m(|u|>R)\le M_eR^{-q_e}.
 \tag{7}
\]
To construct a weakly convergent subsequence directly, diagonally select the distribution functions at the rational numbers.  The monotone rational limits, made right-continuous by taking infima over rationals from the right, define a distribution function \(F\); (7) forces its limits at negative and positive infinity to be zero and one.  At every continuity point of \(F\), rational sandwiching gives convergence of the selected distribution functions to \(F\).  For a bounded continuous function, first use (7) to discard uniformly small tails, then partition the remaining compact interval at continuity points of \(F\), and finally use uniform continuity on each partition interval.  This proves convergence of its integrals and hence weak convergence \(Q_m\Rightarrow Q\) along the selected subsequence.

For \(L<\infty\), the function \(|u|^{q_e}\wedge L\) is bounded and continuous.  Weak convergence and then monotone convergence in \(L\) give
\[
 \int_{\mathbb R}|u|^{q_e}\,dQ(u)
 =\sup_{L<\infty}\int_{\mathbb R}(|u|^{q_e}\wedge L)\,dQ(u)
 \le M_e.
 \tag{8}
\]
For every law in the sequence and for its limit, (8) implies
\[
 \int_{|u|>R}|u|\,dQ(u)
 \le R^{1-q_e}\int_{\mathbb R}|u|^{q_e}\,dQ(u)
 \le M_eR^{1-q_e}.
 \tag{9}
\]
Because \(q_e>1\), the last expression tends to zero.  Apply weak convergence to the bounded continuous clipping of the identity at levels \(-R\) and \(R\), use (9), and then send \(R\to\infty\).  First moments converge.  Therefore the centering condition \(\int u\,dQ_2(u)=0\) is closed.

The same moment restriction supplies both local equicontinuity and the protected neighborhood required by later cocycle arguments; neither is an additional class restriction.  The inequalities \(|e^{isu}-e^{itu}|\le|s-t||u|\), \(|e^{itu}-1|\le|t||u|\), and power mean give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |\phi_{Q_m}(s)-\phi_{Q_m}(t)|
 &\le |s-t|\int|u|\,dQ_m(u)
 \le |s-t|M_e^{1/q_e},\\
 |\phi_Q(t)|
 &\ge 1-|\phi_Q(t)-1|
 \ge 1-|t|\int|u|\,dQ(u)
 \ge 1-|t|M_e^{1/q_e}.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{10}
\]
In particular, with
\[
 \nu_*=(2M_e^{1/q_e})^{-1},\qquad c_*=1/2,
 \tag{11}
\]
every error law in the moment ball obeys \(\inf_{|t|\le\nu_*}|\phi_Q(t)|\ge c_*\).  Weak convergence gives pointwise convergence of characteristic functions because \(u\mapsto e^{itu}\) is bounded and continuous.  The common Lipschitz modulus in (10), applied on a finite frequency mesh, upgrades this convergence to uniform convergence on every compact frequency interval.  Equations (7)--(10) prove sequential compactness and closedness of all restrictions on each error coordinate.  Because weak convergence of probability laws on \(\mathbb R\) is metrized by the metric used in the claim, each error-coordinate set is compact.  Combining the signal, mass, and error coordinates proves compactness of \(\mathscr K\).  Notice that (10)--(11), rather than a separately assumed spectral-modulus condition, give the uniform nonvanishing neighborhood.

Now let \(\vartheta_m\to\vartheta\) in the product metric.  Uniform signal convergence and common support give
\[
 \sup_{r\in\mathbb R}|\widehat f_{x,m}(r)-\widehat f_x(r)|
 \le 2B_A\|f_{x,m}-f_x\|_{L^\infty(\mathcal A)}\longrightarrow0,
 \tag{12}
\]
and the same inequality holds with \(q_x\) in place of \(f_x\).  Local uniform convergence of both error characteristic functions was proved after (10).  Characteristic functions have modulus at most one, \(\int f_x=1\), and \(\int|q_x|\le B_Y\int f_x=B_Y\).  Thus (12) and the triangle inequality for products imply local uniform convergence on \(\mathbb R^2\) of both fitted channels
\[
 (s,t)\longmapsto \widehat f_x(s+t)\phi_{Q_1}(s)\phi_{Q_2}(t),
 \qquad
 (s,t)\longmapsto \widehat q_x(s+t)\phi_{Q_1}(s)\phi_{Q_2}(t).
 \tag{13}
\]

For continuity of the profiled target, the lower bounds \(f_x,f'_x\ge\kappa\) on \(I\) and the domination \(|q'_x|\le B_Yf'_x\), all imposed by \(\textnormal{def:exact-projected-class}\), yield
\[
 \left\|\frac{q_x}{f_x}-\frac{q'_x}{f'_x}\right\|_{L^\infty(I)}
 \le \kappa^{-1}\|q_x-q'_x\|_{L^\infty(\mathcal A)}
     +B_Y\kappa^{-1}\|f_x-f'_x\|_{L^\infty(\mathcal A)}.
 \tag{14}
\]
Moreover, \(\|q'_x/f'_x\|_{L^\infty(I)}\le B_Y\).  The definition \(\mu_\vartheta=\sum_xp_xq_x/f_x\) therefore gives
\[
 \|\mu_\vartheta-\mu_{\vartheta'}\|_{L^\infty(I)}
 \le \sum_xp_x\left\|\frac{q_x}{f_x}-\frac{q'_x}{f'_x}\right\|_{L^\infty(I)}
      +B_Y\sum_x|p_x-p'_x|,
 \tag{15}
\]
which tends to zero in the product metric.  Hence \(\vartheta\mapsto\mu_\vartheta\) is continuous into \(C(I)\).

Finally, fix \(n\) and a realized sample \(z\).  By \(\textnormal{def:exact-joint-feasible-set}\), membership in \(\Theta^{\mathrm{ex}}_{n,\alpha}(z)\) is the conjunction of finitely many mass and channel inequalities.  For example, define
\[
 v^F_{x,s,t}(z,\vartheta)
 =\left(
 \left|\widehat F_{x,n}(z;s,t)
       -\widehat f_x(s+t)\phi_{Q_1}(s)\phi_{Q_2}(t)\right|
       -\rho^F_{x,n}(z)
 \right)_+,
 \tag{16}
\]
with \(v^G_{x,s,t}\) defined analogously, and define the mass violations by
\[
 v^p_x(z,\vartheta)
 =\left(
 |p_x-\widehat p_x(z)|
 -\left\{\frac{\log(6|\mathcal X|/\alpha)}{2n}\right\}^{1/2}
 \right)_+.
 \tag{17}
\]
The empirical sums, counts, empty-cell convention, and radii in \(\textnormal{def:mass-confidence-region}\), \(\textnormal{def:upper-tuning-grid}\), and \(\textnormal{def:ecf-radii}\) are Borel measurable functions of \(z\).  Therefore (16)--(17) are measurable in \(z\).  Equation (13) and continuity of the mass coordinates make them continuous in \(\vartheta\).  Their common zero set is exactly \(\Theta^{\mathrm{ex}}_{n,\alpha}(z)\); it is closed in compact \(\mathscr K\), hence compact.  This also proves the asserted measurability and continuity of every constraint-violation function.

Fix class indices satisfying \(\beta>1/2\) and \(q_e>1\).  For a Borel probability law \(Q_j\) on \(\mathbb R\), put
\(\phi_{Q_j}(t)=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{itu}\,dQ_j(u)\).  The exact projected nuisance class \(\mathscr K\) is the set of tuples
\[
 \vartheta=\bigl((p_x,f_x,q_x)_{x\in\mathcal X},Q_1,Q_2\bigr)
\]
such that
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 p_x\ge p_{\min}\quad(x\in\mathcal X),\qquad
 \sum_{x\in\mathcal X}p_x=1,\\
 f_x:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R,\quad f_x\in H^\beta(\mathbb R),\quad f_x\ge0,\quad
 \int_{\mathbb R}f_x(a)\,da=1,\quad
 \operatorname{supp}(f_x)\subseteq\mathcal A,\quad
 \|f_x\|_{H^\beta}\le R_f,\quad
 \inf_{a\in I}f_x(a)\ge\kappa,\\
 q_x:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R,\quad q_x\in H^\beta(\mathbb R),\quad
 \operatorname{supp}(q_x)\subseteq\mathcal A,\quad
 \|q_x\|_{H^\beta}\le R_q,\quad
 |q_x(a)|\le B_Yf_x(a)\quad(a\in\mathbb R),\\
 \int_{\mathbb R}|u|^{q_e}\,dQ_j(u)\le M_e\quad(j=1,2),\qquad
 \int_{\mathbb R}u\,dQ_2(u)=0.
 \end{gathered}
\]
All pointwise signal constraints use the continuous representatives supplied by \(\beta>1/2\).  The tuple represents the product error law \(Q_1\otimes Q_2\); it is an outer projection of the full causal class and does not assert that every one of its elements has a structural causal realization.  For \(a\in I\), define
\[
 \mu_\vartheta(a)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X}p_x\frac{q_x(a)}{f_x(a)}.
\]

proofs.proof_tex:
Fix two laws \(P^{(0)},P^{(1)}\in\mathcal M\) inducing the same observed law, and fix \(x\in\mathcal X\).  By \(\mathrm{ass{:}strata}\), \(P^{(k)}(X=x)\ge p_{\min}>0\), so both conditional channels \(F_x\) and \(G_x\) are determined by the common observed law.

We first derive, rather than assume, a common nonvanishing neighborhood.  By \(\mathrm{ass{:}error\text{-}moment}\) and the enlarged range \(q_e>1\), the power-mean inequality gives, for \(j\in\{1,2\}\),
\[
 E_{P^{(k)}}|U_j|
 \le \{E_{P^{(k)}}|U_j|^{q_e}\}^{1/q_e}
 \le M_e^{1/q_e}.
 \tag{1}
\]
Since \(|e^{iv}-1|\le |v|\) for real \(v\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |\phi_j^{(k)}(t)|
 &\ge 1-|\phi_j^{(k)}(t)-1|\\
 &\ge 1-E_{P^{(k)}}|e^{itU_j}-1|\\
 &\ge 1-|t|E_{P^{(k)}}|U_j|\\
 &\ge 1-|t|M_e^{1/q_e}.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{2}
\]
Thus, with
\[
 \nu_*=(2M_e^{1/q_e})^{-1},\qquad c_*=\frac12,
 \tag{3}
\]
one has \(|\phi_j^{(k)}(t)|\ge c_*\) whenever \(|t|\le\nu_*\), uniformly in \(j\), \(k\), and the law.  No separate spectral-modulus condition has been used.

Set
\[
 \delta=\min\left\{\nu_*,\frac{1}{4B_A}\right\}>0.
 \tag{4}
\]
Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}compact\text{-}dose}\) says that \(|A|\le B_A\) almost surely.  Hence, for \(|v|\le2\delta\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |\widehat f_x^{(k)}(v)-1|
 &\le \int_{\mathcal A}|e^{iva}-1|f_x^{(k)}(a)\,da\\
 &\le |v|\int_{\mathcal A}|a|f_x^{(k)}(a)\,da\\
 &\le B_A|v|\le\frac12,
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{5}
\]
and therefore \(|\widehat f_x^{(k)}(v)|\ge1/2\).  If \(|u|,|t|\le\delta\), then \(|u+t|\le2\delta\); equations (2), (4), and (5), followed by \(\mathrm{lem{:}factorization}\), yield
\[
 |F_x(u,t)|
 =|\widehat f_x^{(k)}(u+t)\phi_1^{(k)}(u)\phi_2^{(k)}(t)|
 \ge \frac12c_*^2>0.
 \tag{6}
\]

The compact support of \(f_x^{(k)}\) permits differentiation of \(\widehat f_x^{(k)}\), while (1) permits differentiation of \(\phi_2^{(k)}\) at zero by dominated convergence.  Differentiating the factorization in \(\mathrm{lem{:}factorization}\), dividing by (6), and using \(\phi_2^{(k)}(0)=1\), we obtain, for \(|u|\le\delta\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 D_x(u)
 &:=\frac{\left.\partial_tF_x(u,t)\right|_{t=0}}{F_x(u,0)}\\
 &=\frac{(\widehat f_x^{(k)})'(u)}{\widehat f_x^{(k)}(u)}
   +\frac{(\phi_2^{(k)})'(0)}{\phi_2^{(k)}(0)}.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{7}
\]
Equivalently, (7) is the asserted logarithmic derivative for any local continuous branch of the logarithm, whose existence follows from (6).  Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}center\text{-}two}\) and dominated differentiation give
\[
 (\phi_2^{(k)})'(0)=iE_{P^{(k)}}[U_2]=0.
 \tag{8}
\]
The function \(D_x\) is determined solely by the common observed channel.  Equations (7)--(8) therefore imply
\[
 (\widehat f_x^{(k)})'(u)=D_x(u)\widehat f_x^{(k)}(u),
 \qquad \widehat f_x^{(k)}(0)=1.
 \tag{9}
\]
Because the denominator is nonzero by (5), the ratio
\(R(u)=\widehat f_x^{(1)}(u)/\widehat f_x^{(0)}(u)\) is differentiable on \([-\delta,\delta]\).  Equation (9) gives \(R'(u)=0\), and normalization gives \(R(0)=1\).  Consequently
\[
 \widehat f_x^{(1)}(u)=\widehat f_x^{(0)}(u),
 \qquad |u|\le\delta.
 \tag{10}
\]
This calculation never differentiates \(\phi_1\), so it imposes no location normalization on \(U_1\).

We next extend (10) globally without assuming global nonvanishing of either error transform.  Compact support gives, for every complex \(z\),
\[
 \sum_{r=0}^{\infty}\frac{|z|^r}{r!}
 \int_{\mathcal A}|a|^rf_x^{(k)}(a)\,da
 \le e^{B_A|z|}.
 \tag{11}
\]
Tonelli's theorem and (11) justify termwise integration of the exponential series, so
\[
 \widehat f_x^{(k)}(z)
 =\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}\frac{(iz)^r}{r!}
   \int_{\mathcal A}a^rf_x^{(k)}(a)\,da,
 \qquad z\in\mathbb C.
 \tag{12}
\]
Thus each transform is entire.  The difference of the transforms in (10) is zero on a real neighborhood of zero, so all of its real derivatives at zero vanish.  Those derivatives equal the complex derivatives supplied by (12); hence every coefficient of its globally convergent power series is zero.  It follows that
\[
 \widehat f_x^{(1)}(z)=\widehat f_x^{(0)}(z),
 \qquad z\in\mathbb C.
 \tag{13}
\]

For the marked channel, put \(t=0\) in the two identities of \(\mathrm{lem{:}factorization}\).  Since \(F_x(u,0)\ne0\) for \(|u|\le\delta\), division is legitimate and gives, under either candidate law,
\[
 \widehat q_x^{(k)}(u)
 =\widehat f_x^{(k)}(u)\frac{G_x(u,0)}{F_x(u,0)},
 \qquad |u|\le\delta.
 \tag{14}
\]
The right-hand side is the same for \(k=0,1\) by the common observed law and (10).  Hence the two marked transforms agree locally.  Assumptions \(\mathrm{ass{:}consistency}\) and \(\mathrm{ass{:}bounded\text{-}outcome}\) imply \(|Y|\le B_Y\) almost surely and therefore \(|m_x(a)|\le B_Y\) for \(f_x(a)\,da\)-almost every \(a\).  Since \(q_x=m_xf_x\),
\[
 |q_x(a)|\le B_Yf_x(a)\quad\text{almost everywhere},
 \qquad \operatorname{supp}(q_x)\subseteq\mathcal A,
 \qquad \|q_x\|_1\le B_Y.
 \tag{15}
\]
Replacing \(f_x^{(k)}\) by \(q_x^{(k)}\) and the right side of (11) by \(B_Ye^{B_A|z|}\) proves that \(\widehat q_x^{(k)}\) is entire.  The power-series argument used for (13), now starting from the local equality implied by (14), yields
\[
 \widehat q_x^{(1)}(z)=\widehat q_x^{(0)}(z),
 \qquad z\in\mathbb C.
 \tag{16}
\]

For completeness, we verify that equality of transforms identifies the underlying functions.  Let \(h\) be the difference of the two candidate \(f_x\)'s or of the two candidate \(q_x\)'s.  Equations (13) and (16) give \(\widehat h(t)=0\) for every real \(t\), while compact support and (15) give \(h\in L^1(\mathbb R)\).  For \(\epsilon>0\), define
\[
 g_\epsilon(v)=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-1/2}e^{-v^2/(2\epsilon)}
 =\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-itv}e^{-\epsilon t^2/2}\,dt.
 \tag{17}
\]
Fubini's theorem applies because \(h\in L^1\) and the Gaussian multiplier is integrable.  Therefore
\[
 (h*g_\epsilon)(a)
 =\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-ita}\widehat h(t)
       e^{-\epsilon t^2/2}\,dt=0.
 \tag{18}
\]
Translation is continuous in \(L^1\): it is immediate for compactly supported step functions, and the general case follows by approximating \(h\) in \(L^1\), because translation preserves the \(L^1\)-norm.  Consequently
\[
 \|h*g_\epsilon-h\|_1
 \le\int_{\mathbb R}g_\epsilon(v)
       \|h(\mathord\cdot-v)-h\|_1\,dv\longrightarrow0.
 \tag{19}
\]
Indeed, on a fixed neighborhood of zero the integrand in (19) is uniformly small by translation continuity, outside that neighborhood it is at most \(2\|h\|_1\), and the Gaussian mass there tends to zero.  Equations (18)--(19) imply \(h=0\) almost everywhere.

Finally, \(\mathrm{ass{:}f\text{-}sobolev}\), \(\mathrm{ass{:}q\text{-}sobolev}\), and the enlarged range \(\beta>1/2\) select unique continuous representatives.  In fact, for either difference \(h\), Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 \int_{\mathbb R}|\widehat h(t)|\,dt
 \le
 \left\{\int_{\mathbb R}(1+t^2)^\beta|\widehat h(t)|^2\,dt\right\}^{1/2}
 \left\{\int_{\mathbb R}(1+t^2)^{-\beta}\,dt\right\}^{1/2}<\infty.
 \tag{20}
\]
Fourier inversion therefore supplies a continuous representative, and a continuous function that is zero almost everywhere is zero everywhere.  Thus \(f_x^{(0)}=f_x^{(1)}\) and \(q_x^{(0)}=q_x^{(1)}\).  Since \(x\) was arbitrary, the common observed law identifies all \(\{(f_x,q_x):x\in\mathcal X\}\).  Equations (2)--(3) show that this conclusion permits open spectral zero sets away from zero and requires no separately assumed local modulus.

proposed.statement: The map \(P\mapsto P_{\mathrm{obs}}\) is injective for \(\{(f_x,q_x):x\in\mathcal X\}\) over \(\mathcal M\). On a common neighborhood of zero, \(\left.\partial_t\log F_x(u,t)\right|_{t=0}=\widehat f_x'(u)/\widehat f_x(u)+\phi_2'(0)=\widehat f_x'(u)/\widehat f_x(u)\), because \(\phi_2(0)=1\) and \(\phi_2'(0)=iE_P[U_2]=0\). Together with \(\widehat f_x(0)=1\), this derivative identity uniquely fixes the latent translation without a normalization on \(U_1\). Moreover, \(\widehat q_x(u)=\widehat f_x(u)G_x(u,0)/F_x(u,0)\). Compact support makes both recovered transforms entire, so the local formulas determine \(f_x\) and \(q_x\) globally even when either error transform has an open zero set away from zero.
